source_document.body:
Few topics in transportation draw more attention right now than artificial intelligence. Carriers want to know what it means for their workforce and their bottom line, and the loudest version of the debate asks whether AI will replace the people who run trucking operations.
Danielle Villegas, chief product and technology officer at PCS Software, Inc., has a different framing. In an appearance on FreightWaves’ What the Truck?!? , she described AI as a force multiplier: a tool that takes on repetitive work so people can spend their time on decisions that matter.
“It really just multiplies the efficiency of your team versus replacing anybody that you have,” Villegas said.
Automating the routine, freeing the dispatcher
For Villegas, the starting point is identifying the tasks dispatchers repeat every day. Routine notifications, such as on-time or delayed delivery updates, and load entry are prime candidates. Automating them gives dispatchers room to find more freight and handle exceptions, like a truck breaking down and a replacement driver having to be arranged.
That approach also changes what AI is for. Rather than treating it only as a way to cut costs, Villegas frames it as a way to expand what a dispatch team can do, from workforce capacity to revenue potential. Her description of the work AI should absorb is blunt: “letting AI do all of those boring, mundane things for you.”
Why the human stays accountable
The efficiency case comes with a caveat. Villegas said anyone who has spent time with AI tools knows their limits. “Sometimes AI is confidently wrong when it’s wrong,” she said.
That is why PCS builds its products around human oversight, particularly for consequential decisions. “You have to keep the human in the loop, especially when dollars or safety is concerned,” Villegas said.
Rates are the clearest example. If an AI system proposes the wrong one, the effect lands directly on the bottom line. “Margins are thin, especially for carriers,” she said. Her model is for AI to make recommendations and speed up decisions while a person makes the final call: “There’s a human pressing that button, saying, ‘Yep, that’s the right rate.’”
To explain why visibility matters, Villegas pointed to the camera inside a Waymo. The passenger display isn’t there because the vehicle needs it. It’s there to build confidence. “It gives you the confidence that the Waymo sees the person crossing the street,” she said. The same logic applies in freight, where users need to see what the AI is proposing and why.
Inside Cortex: 40-plus data elements
That transparency principle shapes how PCS designed driver assignment in Cortex. According to Villegas, the feature draws on more than 40 data elements to recommend which driver should haul which load. Those inputs include dispatcher knowledge, hours of service , stop times, how far a driver is willing to travel and whether the driver needs to get home.
Dispatcher history matters because, as Villegas put it, “there’s going to be knowledge inside of a dispatcher’s head that no technology, no LLM, no software in the world is ever going to have.”
The system then shows its work. Users can see the margin and the deadhead they would take on with a given driver. Cortex can also evaluate loads together rather than one at a time. “If you put three loads together, you’re going to reduce your deadhead,” Villegas said, noting that a load-by-load view might miss the combination entirely.
An assist, not a hostile takeover
Villegas said the line for AI autonomy comes down to explainability. If a system can’t show where its recommendation came from, users should question it. She added that the stakes are higher because AI isn’t only available to legitimate operators.
“It cannot be a black box because not only the good guys are using AI, the bad guys are using it as well,” she said.
Her prescription is visibility plus control. “You have to have that visibility, and you have to be able to turn it off,” Villegas said. She was equally direct about the role AI should play: “It’s an assist and not a hostile takeover. If it’s a hostile takeover, you can’t have that accountability.”
Meeting customers where they are
Through PCS’s early adopter program, Villegas said, the company has learned that customers vary widely in how much automation they want. Some welcome AI that builds a load from a PDF, work that spares dispatchers from keying it in by hand. Others want AI to reach out on its own, without a person clicking a button.
PCS’s answer is a configurable, rules-based approach that determines when AI assists and when it acts. “Each customer is different,” Villegas said, and the pace varies: “Some of them want to crawl before they run, and some of them want to run.”
Customer attitudes have shifted as well. When PCS first introduced Cora, its voice AI agent, interest was low. “Nope, AI voice agents. I don’t want to talk to them,” Villegas said, recalling the early reaction. Today, she said, the request is different. “I want more Cora,” customers tell her. In her words, “It’s a choose-your-own-adventure.”
Finding backhauls without losing control
One of Cora’s uses is backhaul outreach. Villegas said PCS’s market research found customers losing hundreds of thousands of dollars because they lacked the dispatch staff to find return loads, leaving trucks to run empty to the next pickup. The system identifies opportunities, including through load board connections, and Cora can make high-volume calls to freight sources far faster than a dispatcher placing one call at a time.
Even here, a person stays in charge. Cora assembles opportunities for review rather than dispatching anything on its own. “It’s not a load that automatically comes in that says, ‘Hey, this is getting dispatched,’” Villegas said. “You get to check the rate. You get to make sure all the details make sense before you’re putting a driver onto that backhaul.”
Practicing what PCS preaches
PCS applies the same principle inside its own walls. Villegas said the company rolled out Claude internally and let AI handle tasks like drafting software tickets and tracking customer issues and planned enhancements, with people reviewing the results and the testing. She described the path to getting value as hands-on. “I think it’s just a lot of trial and error, to be completely honest, and leaning into it,” she said.
The message to customers is the same one PCS follows itself: “Let your people manage the exceptions and let the AI manage those routine tasks.”
The question to ask every AI vendor
With new AI vendors appearing constantly, Villegas was asked what question a trucking company should put to one before signing. Her answer centered on proof. “What are the results it’s going to give me, and how do I know that it’s working?” she said, adding, “Show me why you got that result.”
She said buyers should also ask which of their own data a vendor’s system relies on. “AI is only as smart as the data it has access to,” Villegas said.
Where the human-AI relationship goes next
Looking ahead, Villegas expects progress to come through trust, not sudden disruption. “I think it’s really kind of building the trust with it,” she said. “I think it’s going to be a little slow at first.”
As users get comfortable, she expects the way they work with transportation management software to change. “It kind of becomes more of a headless application more than anything else,” Villegas said, adding that shippers and carriers will demand more from their software vendors. The change isn’t limited to developers, either. “I’ve got truckers that are vibe coding out there right now,” she said.
That momentum raises the importance of guardrails. “You don’t want AI to run rampant,” Villegas said. For any vendor, she said, the safeguards come back to the same few principles: “You have to be able to turn it off. You have to have that human in the loop.”
Her closing point returned to accountability. “Someone has to be able to control it,” Villegas said.
